claim: Oculomotor circuits take into consideration the physical salience of objects in view and current behavioral goals when generating the next eye movement.
source: To generate the next eye movement, oculomotor circuits take into consideration the physical salience of objects in view and current behavioral goals, exogenous and endogenous influences, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about oculomotor function in the abstract.

claim: The exogenous signal arrives approximately 80 ms after cue onset in the urgent antisaccade task.
source: Empirical and modeling results indicated that the exogenous signal arrives ∼80 ms after cue onset and rapidly accelerates the (incorrect) plan toward the cue, whereas the informed endogenous signal arrives ∼25 ms later to favor the (correct) plan away from the cue.
evidence: This timing is derived from empirical data and modeling results from the cited study (Salinas et al., 2019).

claim: The informed endogenous signal arrives approximately 25 ms after the exogenous signal.
source: Empirical and modeling results indicated that the exogenous signal arrives ∼80 ms after cue onset and rapidly accelerates the (incorrect) plan toward the cue, whereas the informed endogenous signal arrives ∼25 ms later to favor the (correct) plan away from the cue.
evidence: This timing is derived from empirical data and modeling results from the cited study.

claim: The exogenous and endogenous signals act at different times and independently of each other.
source: Here, we scrutinize a key mechanistic hypothesis about this dynamic, that the exogenous and endogenous signals act at different times and independently of each other.
evidence: This is stated as the key hypothesis being tested in the current study.

claim: The exogenous response is largely impervious to task instructions.
source: We find that, indeed, the exogenous response is largely impervious to task instructions; it simply flips its sign relative to the correct choice, and this largely explains the drastic differences in psychometric performance between the two tasks.
evidence: This is a main finding from the experimental data comparing pro- and antisaccade tasks.

claim: The exogenous response flips its sign relative to the correct choice between pro- and antisaccade tasks.
source: We find that, indeed, the exogenous response is largely impervious to task instructions; it simply flips its sign relative to the correct choice, and this largely explains the drastic differences in psychometric performance between the two tasks.
evidence: This is a main finding from the experimental data.

claim: Saccadic choices are strongly dictated by the alignment between salience and behavioral goals.
source: Thus, saccadic choices are strongly dictated by the alignment between salience and behavioral goals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The oculomotor system of primates specifies a new target to look at every 200–250 ms.
source: The oculomotor system of primates specifies a new target to look at every 200–250 ms.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about primate oculomotor behavior.

claim: Exogenous mechanisms respond to the salience of objects in view, typically dictated by physical properties such as size, luminance, or motion.
source: Two components of visuospatial attention contribute to the underlying selection process: exogenous mechanisms, which respond to the salience of the objects in view (typically dictated by physical properties such as size, luminance, or motion), and endogenous mechanisms, which prioritize those objects according to their relevance to current behavioral goals (Itti and Koch, 2001; Theeuwes, 2010; Wolfe and Horowitz, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on visuospatial attention.

claim: Endogenous mechanisms prioritize objects according to their relevance to current behavioral goals.
source: Two components of visuospatial attention contribute to the underlying selection process: exogenous mechanisms, which respond to the salience of the objects in view (typically dictated by physical properties such as size, luminance, or motion), and endogenous mechanisms, which prioritize those objects according to their relevance to current behavioral goals (Itti and Koch, 2001; Theeuwes, 2010; Wolfe and Horowitz, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on visuospatial attention.

claim: The antisaccade task is ideal for examining the distinction between exogenous and endogenous mechanisms because it decouples stimulus encoding and response preparation.
source: The antisaccade task, in which the subject is required to look away from a lone visual cue, is ideal for examining this distinction because it decouples stimulus encoding and response preparation (Munoz and Everling, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Munoz and Everling, 2004.

claim: For a correct antisaccade to take place, endogenous, top-down influences must override the natural tendency to look to the cue.
source: For a correct antisaccade to take place, endogenous, top-down influences must override the natural tendency to look to the cue.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about antisaccade performance.

claim: Antisaccade performance is generally characterized as a conflict between volitional and sensory-driven, reflexive responses in both imaging studies in humans and single-neuron recordings in nonhuman primates.
source: Indeed, in both imaging studies in humans (Brown et al., 2007; Anderson et al., 2008) and single-neuron recordings in nonhuman primates (Everling et al., 1998; Everling et al., 1999; Everling and Munoz, 2000), antisaccade performance is generally characterized as a conflict between volitional and sensory-driven, reflexive responses.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to imaging and neurophysiology studies.

claim: Reaction time and accuracy measurements in the antisaccade task are commonly used as clinical markers for cognitive dysfunction.
source: The capacity to resolve such conflict is considered so fundamental, that reaction time (RT) and accuracy measurements in the antisaccade task are commonly used as clinical markers for cognitive dysfunction (Klein and Foerster, 2001; Klein et al., 2003; Hutton and Ettinger, 2006; Fielding et al., 2009; Johansson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: The urgent antisaccade task revealed a range of processing times roughly between 90 and 130 ms in which performance plummeted to nearly 0% correct.
source: In the urgent antisaccade experiment (Salinas et al., 2019), the tachometric curve revealed a unique feature: a range of processing times roughly between 90 and 130 ms in which performance plummeted to nearly 0% correct (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is based on data from the cited study and shown in Figure 2d.

claim: After rPT ≳140 ms in the urgent antisaccade task, accuracy increased steadily and reached nearly 100% correct.
source: Thereafter, for rPT ≳140 ms, accuracy increased steadily and reached nearly 100% correct.
evidence: This is based on data from the urgent antisaccade experiment.

claim: The CAS model quantitatively replicated the full range of psychophysical results obtained in the urgent antisaccade task.
source: With these elements in place, the CAS model was able to reproduce the full range of psychophysical results obtained in the urgent antisaccade task, both on average and in individual participants (with parameter values adjusted accordingly; Salinas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on modeling results from the cited study.

claim: The CAS model accurately replicated the full RT distributions for correct and error trials.
source: In particular, it quantitatively matched the full RT distributions for correct and error trials (see Figure 8 and its supplements in Salinas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on modeling results from the cited study.

claim: The initial departure from chance in prosaccade performance follows the same timecourse as the initial downswing in antisaccade performance but in opposite directions.
source: The first one is that the upswing in performance during prosaccade trials should follow the same timecourse as the initial downswing in performance during antisaccade trials (Figure 3a, b). In other words, the initial departure from chance should exhibit the same dependence on rPT but going in opposite directions, toward 100% versus toward 0% correct.
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 3a, b.

claim: During antisaccade trials with the cue on the preferred guessing side, the rise in success rate is expected to occur late.
source: If such a bias exists, then during antisaccade trials in which the cue happens to appear on the preferred guessing side, the rise in success rate is expected to occur late (Figure 3c, red trace).
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 3c.

claim: During antisaccade trials with the cue opposite to the preferred guessing side, the success rate should rise earlier.
source: In contrast, during antisaccade trials in which the cue happens to appear opposite to the preferred guessing side, the success rate should rise earlier (Figure 3c, black trace).
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 3c.

claim: During prosaccade trials, the rise in success rate is expected to be very similar regardless of where the cue appears relative to the guessing direction.
source: On the other hand, during prosaccade trials the rise in success rate is expected to be very similar regardless of where the cue appears relative to the guessing direction (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Ten participants (6 female, 4 male) were recruited for the experiment.
source: To test the model predictions, 10 participants (6 female, 4 male) were recruited.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The pooled tachometric curve for the compelled antisaccade task exhibited the characteristic drop in success rate due to potent oculomotor capture in the range between 90 and 140 ms.
source: For the compelled antisaccade task, the pooled tachometric curve (Figure 4a, red trace), generated by combining the data across participants, replicated our earlier result (Salinas et al., 2019). It exhibited the characteristic drop in success rate due to potent oculomotor capture in the range between 90 and 140 ms, approximately, with the subsequent recovery reaching nearly 100% correct after ∼200 ms of cue viewing time.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: For the compelled prosaccade task, the success rate rose steadily, early, and very steeply.
source: More importantly, for the compelled prosaccade task the shape of the pooled tachometric curve (Figure 4a, blue trace) was as predicted by the model. In this case, the success rate rose steadily, early, and very steeply.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The optimal time shift between the upswing in prosaccade performance and the downswing in antisaccade performance was 3 ms with a 95% confidence interval of [1, 5] ms.
source: Whereas according to the prediction the optimal time shift should be zero (Figure 3b, arrow), experimentally, we found that the optimal shift was, on average, 3 ms within a 95% confidence interval (CI) of [1, 5] ms (Figure 4b, d).
evidence: This is based on experimental data analysis shown in Figure 4b, d.

claim: In prosaccade trials, the effect of the exogenous response manifested about 3 ms earlier than in antisaccade trials.
source: That is, in prosaccade trials, the effect of the exogenous response manifested about 3 ms earlier than in antisaccade trials.
evidence: This is based on the optimal shift analysis of experimental data.

claim: Individual participants had optimal shifts in the [−1, 10] ms range.
source: This time difference was of comparable magnitude across individual participants (Figure 4c), which had optimal shifts in the [−1, 10] ms range (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4c, d.

claim: In the antisaccade task, less luminant cues produce capture at longer processing times.
source: We knew that, in the antisaccade task, less luminant cues produce capture at longer processing times (Salinas et al., 2019), so we reasoned that the rise in prosaccade performance should demonstrate the same temporal dependence — if it is driven by the same exogenous signal.
evidence: This is based on data from the cited study.

claim: In antisaccade trials, the decrease in cue luminance resulted in a rightward shift of the tachometric curve of 35 ms ([33, 38] ms 95% CI).
source: As expected, in antisaccade trials the decrease in cue luminance resulted in a rightward shift of the tachometric curve (Figure 4e, red curves), which was of 35 ms ([33, 38] ms 95% CI), as determined by an optimal-shift analysis.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: In prosaccade trials, lower luminance resulted in a shift of 30 ms ([26, 34] ms 95% CI).
source: And critically, a comparable delay was observed in prosaccade trials (Figure 4e, blue curves), for which the lower luminance resulted in a shift of 30 ms ([26, 34] ms 95% CI).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Participants' guesses in a given trial were generally toward the location where they should have responded in the previous trial.
source: When we analyzed our participants' performance as a function of their prior choices, we noticed a trend: their guesses in a given trial were generally toward the location where they should have responded in the previous trial (i.e., the prior target location).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: The tachometric curve conditioned on a repeated target location demonstrated a positive offset above chance in the range of processing times for which participants must guess (rPT ≲80 ms).
source: Specifically, the tachometric curve conditioned on a repeated target location (Figure 5a, green trace) demonstrated a positive offset (above chance) in the range of processing times for which participants must guess (rPT ≲80 ms), whereas the tachometric curve conditioned on a switch in target location (Figure 5a, magenta trace) demonstrated a negative offset (below chance) in the same range.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The motor bias effect was cumulative; the more target repetitions, the larger the offsets.
source: This effect was cumulative; the more target repetitions, the larger the offsets (Figure 5, compare across columns).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The motor bias effect was observed in most participants and in both pro and anti trials.
source: It was also observed in most participants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and in both pro and anti trials.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the antisaccade task, the rise toward asymptotic performance occurred late when the motor bias was aligned with the cue location and early when it was aligned with the anti location.
source: We found that both aspects of the second model prediction were correct. In the antisaccade task, the rise toward asymptotic performance occurred late when the motor bias was aligned with the cue location (Figure 5a–c, magenta curves) and early when it was aligned with the anti, or target location (Figure 5a–c, green curves); whereas in the prosaccade task, the rise was essentially the same in the two cases (Figure 5d–f).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5a–c.

claim: In the prosaccade task, the rise toward asymptotic performance was essentially the same regardless of motor bias direction.
source: We found that both aspects of the second model prediction were correct. In the antisaccade task, the rise toward asymptotic performance occurred late when the motor bias was aligned with the cue location (Figure 5a–c, magenta curves) and early when it was aligned with the anti, or target location (Figure 5a–c, green curves); whereas in the prosaccade task, the rise was essentially the same in the two cases (Figure 5d–f).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5d–f.

claim: As the chance level went from 0.36 to 0.64, the rise point of the tachometric curve went from 154 ms to 143 ms in antisaccade trials conditioned on one previous trial.
source: Consider the tachometric curves conditioned on one previous trial (Figure 5a). As the chance level went from 0.36 ([0.34, 0.39] 95% CI, AB trials) to 0.64 ([0.61, 0.66], AA trials), the rise point of the tachometric curve went from 154 ms ([149, 154] CI, AB trials) to 143 ms ([139, 144], AA trials).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The predicted change in rise point over the full chance range was 40 ms ([36, 44] 95% CI) according to model simulations.
source: According to this procedure, the predicted change in rise point over the full chance range was 40 ms ([36, 44] 95% CI; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b, blue line and circles), in excellent agreement with the experimental data.
evidence: This is based on model simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: For the antisaccade task, the drop point ranged from 87 to 98 ms across individual participants.
source: Across the individual curves, the drop point (the rPT for which the success rate is halfway between chance and the minimum; Materials and methods) ranged from 87 to 98 ms, whereas the rise point ranged from 133 to 203 ms.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from individual participants.

claim: For the antisaccade task, the rise point ranged from 133 to 203 ms across individual participants.
source: Across the individual curves, the drop point (the rPT for which the success rate is halfway between chance and the minimum; Materials and methods) ranged from 87 to 98 ms, whereas the rise point ranged from 133 to 203 ms.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from individual participants.

claim: For the prosaccade task, the rise point covered a range from 82 to 95 ms across participants.
source: For the prosaccade task, the rise point covered a range from 82 to 95 ms across participants (Figure 6b), similar to that of the drop point in the anti task.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Participants that showed an earlier departure from chance in one task also showed an earlier departure from chance in the other task.
source: In summary, then, participants that showed an earlier departure from chance in one task also showed an earlier departure from chance in the other, consistent with the notion that, for each individual, the exogenous capture is fundamentally the same in the two tasks.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: When saccade-related neural activity is ramping up, the cue onset can accelerate that activity past the threshold beyond which a saccade is inevitably produced before top-down information can influence the choice.
source: Given our modeling framework, the mechanistic intuition behind these results is straightforward: when saccade-related neural activity is ramping up, the cue onset can accelerate that activity past the threshold beyond which a saccade is inevitably produced — before top-down information can influence the choice.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the modeling framework.

claim: The eye movement is elicited very rapidly, after 75–100 ms of viewing time in captured saccades.
source: In either case, the eye movement is elicited very rapidly, after 75–100 ms of viewing time.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Exogenous capture potentially encompasses oculomotor capture, express saccades, exogenous attention, and attentional capture.
source: Understood this way — as an involuntary and stereotypical bias on motor planning that occurs when a stimulus is detected by oculomotor circuits — exogenous capture potentially encompasses a wide range of oculomotor phenomena (Salinas and Stanford, 2021). These include (1) oculomotor capture itself, which is observed when saccades are overtly directed toward salient distracters (Theeuwes et al., 1998; Theeuwes et al., 1999); (2) express saccades, which are saccades triggered with extremely short latencies (Kalesnykas and Hallett, 1987; Paré and Munoz, 1996; Sparks et al., 2000); (3) exogenous attention, which improves perceptual performance at explicitly cued locations (Carrasco, 2011) and has neural correlates that are highly consistent with our framework (Bisley and Goldberg, 2003; Busse et al., 2008; Herrington and Assad, 2010); and (4) attentional capture, which is typically observed when saccades to a target take longer in the presence of salient distracters (Ruz and Lupiáñez, 2002; Theeuwes, 2010).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Oculomotor capture is observed when saccades are overtly directed toward salient distracters.
source: (1) oculomotor capture itself, which is observed when saccades are overtly directed toward salient distracters (Theeuwes et al., 1998; Theeuwes et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Express saccades are saccades triggered with extremely short latencies.
source: (2) express saccades, which are saccades triggered with extremely short latencies (Kalesnykas and Hallett, 1987; Paré and Munoz, 1996; Sparks et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Exogenous attention improves perceptual performance at explicitly cued locations.
source: (3) exogenous attention, which improves perceptual performance at explicitly cued locations (Carrasco, 2011) and has neural correlates that are highly consistent with our framework (Bisley and Goldberg, 2003; Busse et al., 2008; Herrington and Assad, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Attentional capture is typically observed when saccades to a target take longer in the presence of salient distracters.
source: (4) attentional capture, which is typically observed when saccades to a target take longer in the presence of salient distracters (Ruz and Lupiáñez, 2002; Theeuwes, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: When motor plans are already underway, exogenous capture becomes strong and highly reliable.
source: When motor plans are already underway, exogenous capture becomes strong and highly reliable, and its impact on performance easier to discern across tasks (Salinas et al., 2019; Oor et al., 2021; Salinas and Stanford, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Robust capture phenomena can be generated in urgent tasks that use button presses instead of saccades.
source: Work by Poth, 2021 showed that robust capture phenomena can be generated in urgent tasks that use button presses instead of saccades and impose very different cognitive demands on the choice process.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Poth, 2021.

claim: Success in the antisaccade task is typically conceptualized as the result of inhibitory control.
source: Success in the antisaccade task is typically conceptualized as the result of inhibitory control. That is, it is assumed that an inhibitory process suppresses the reflexive reaction of looking at the suddenly appearing visual cue (Munoz and Everling, 2004; Wiecki and Frank, 2013; Coe and Munoz, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Weaker preparatory activity, due to a late break of fixation or to low urgency to respond, leads to lower probability of capture on average.
source: On average, weaker preparatory activity, due to a late break of fixation or to low urgency to respond, leads to lower probability of capture, consistent with single-neuron recordings in the superior colliculus and the frontal eye field (Everling et al., 1999; Everling and Munoz, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neurophysiology studies.

claim: A developing motor plan that is spatially incongruent with the cue is less likely to be captured than one that is congruent.
source: A developing motor plan that, by chance, is spatially incongruent with the cue is less likely to be captured than one that is congruent (Figure 5a–c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), also in agreement with neural recordings (Everling et al., 1998; Everling et al., 1999; Everling and Munoz, 2000).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and supported by citations to neurophysiology studies.

claim: Less salient cues lead to later and less pronounced capture.
source: The intensity of the exogenous response is certainly critical, with less salient cues leading to later and less pronounced capture (Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Salinas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 3, and supported by citation.

claim: There is no mechanism for preventing the exogenous burst; at most it may be slightly modulated by task conditions.
source: But as far as we can tell, there is no mechanism for preventing the exogenous burst; at most it may be slightly modulated by task conditions (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Everling et al., 1998; Everling and Munoz, 2000; see also Gu et al., 2016; Salinas and Stanford, 2018, Salinas et al., 2019; Buonocore et al., 2017; Bompas et al., 2020; Salinas and Stanford, 2021).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The endogenous modulation that steers the motor plans must decelerate the incorrect motor plan.
source: Finally, the probability of a successful antisaccade is higher when the endogenous modulation that steers the motor plans is stronger or arrives earlier. This signal does implicate inhibition because it must decelerate the incorrect motor plan, but according to modeling results, this applies equally to any urgent saccadic choice that is perceptually informed (Stanford et al., 2010; Shankar et al., 2011; Costello et al., 2013; Salinas and Stanford, 2013; Salinas and Stanford, 2018; Salinas and Stanford, 2021; Seideman et al., 2018; Stanford and Salinas, 2021), including prosaccades.
evidence: This is based on modeling results supported by multiple citations.

claim: Endogenous inhibition complements endogenous excitation that is necessary for accelerating the correct motor plan.
source: Furthermore, endogenous inhibition does not act alone, it complements endogenous excitation that is necessary for accelerating the correct motor plan.
evidence: This is based on the modeling framework.

claim: The capture mechanism is the same in the urgent pro- and antisaccade tasks.
source: In summary, then, we found that the capture mechanism is the same in the urgent pro- and antisaccade tasks, and that it is the consequence of a robust exogenous burst of oculomotor activity that always occurs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The exogenous burst of oculomotor activity always occurs in urgent pro- and antisaccade tasks.
source: In summary, then, we found that the capture mechanism is the same in the urgent pro- and antisaccade tasks, and that it is the consequence of a robust exogenous burst of oculomotor activity that always occurs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: All experimental subjects were healthy human volunteers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: Experimental subjects were 10 healthy human volunteers, 4 male and 6 female, with a median age of 28 and ranging between 22 and 63 years. They were recruited from the Wake Forest School of Medicine and Wake Forest University communities. All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The experiment took place in a semi-dark room with participants viewing stimuli on a VIEWPixx LED monitor at a distance of 57 cm.
source: As in the preceding study (Salinas et al., 2019), the experiment took place in a semi-dark room. The participants sat on an adjustable chair, with their chin and forehead supported, and viewed stimuli presented on a VIEWPixx LED monitor (VPixx Technologies Inc, Saint Bruno, Quebec, Canada; 1920 × 1200 screen resolution, 120 Hz refresh rate, 12-bit color) at a distance of 57 cm.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: Eye position was recorded using an EyeLink 1000 infrared camera and tracking system at 1000 Hz sampling rate.
source: Eye position was recorded using an EyeLink 1000 infrared camera and tracking system (SR Research, Ottawa, Canada; 1000 Hz sampling rate).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The cue was a circle of 1.5° diameter.
source: The cue was a circle of 1.5° diameter.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Auditory feedback (a beep) was provided at the end of the trial if the saccadic choice was made within the allowed RT window (425 ms).
source: Auditory feedback (a beep) was provided at the end of the trial if the saccadic choice was made within the allowed RT window (425 ms); no sound was played if the limit was exceeded.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: No feedback was given about the correctness of the spatial choice.
source: No feedback was given about the correctness of the spatial choice.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: For half of the participants (P1–P5), the cue was green in prosaccade trials and magenta in antisaccade trials.
source: For half of the participants (P1–P5), the cue was green (RGB vector [0 0.88 0]) in prosaccade trials and magenta (RGB vector [1 0.32 1]) in antisaccade trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: For the other half of participants (P6–P10), the color assignments were swapped.
source: For the other half (P6–P10), the color assignments were swapped.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The green and magenta stimuli had the same luminance (48 cd m−2).
source: The green and magenta stimuli had the same luminance (48 cd m−2), as determined by a spectrophotometer (i1 Pro 2 from X-Rite, Inc, Grand Rapids, MI).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: In the secondary experiment, the task type (pro or anti) and cue luminance (high or low) were independently sampled in each trial.
source: In this case, however, in each trial, the task type (pro or anti) and cue luminance (high or low) were independently sampled, so the four possible combinations were randomly interleaved.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for the secondary experiment.

claim: The green and magenta cues of low luminance had a luminance of 0.24 cd m−2.
source: The green (RGB vector [0 0.0733 0]) and magenta (RGB vector [0.0833 0.0267 0.833]) cues of low luminance (0.24 cd m−2) were chosen so that significant rightward shifts of the tachometric curve would be generated (Salinas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli in the secondary experiment.

claim: All results are based on the analysis of urgent trials (gap ≥0) only; easy, nonurgent trials (gap <0) were excluded.
source: All results are based on the analysis of urgent trials (gap ≥0) only; easy, nonurgent trials (gap <0) were excluded.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The RT was always measured as the time elapsed between the go signal (fixation offset) and saccade onset.
source: The RT was always measured as the time elapsed between the go signal (fixation offset) and saccade onset (equal to the first time point after the go for which the eye velocity exceeded a threshold of 40°/s).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: Processing times were computed as rPT = RT – gap.
source: Processing times were computed as rPT = RT – gap, where all quantities are specific to each trial.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: During the exogenous response interval (ERI), the motor plan toward the cue is first briefly halted and then accelerated in the CAS model.
source: Specifically, this means that, during the ERI, the motor plan toward the cue is first briefly halted and then accelerated (Figure 2b, c, red traces during gray interval), whereas the motor plan toward the opposite, or 'anti', location is halted throughout (Figure 2b, c, black traces during gray interval).
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism shown in Figure 2b, c.

claim: After the ERI ends in the CAS model, the plan toward the cue is decelerated and the plan away from the cue is accelerated.
source: Then, after the ERI ends, once the cue location has been interpreted in accordance to task rules as 'opposite to the target', the motor selection process is steered toward the correct choice. Specifically, the (erroneous) plan toward the cue is decelerated (Figure 2c, red trace after gray interval) and the (correct) plan away from the cue is accelerated (Figure 2c, black trace after gray interval).
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism shown in Figure 2c.
